items.author: Richard MacManus
items.subtitle: Latent Space
items.title: The Jev Revolution: What Engineers Are Already Building with System One Models
items.excerpt: Today at the AI Engineer Code Summit , the main theme was system one models — non-generative models that return structured choices, scores, or probabilities. They’re also typically much faster and cheaper than reasoning LLMs (a.k.a. system two models). And who better to give an inspirational rallying cry for system one models than Diogo Almeida , co-founder and CEO of TypeSafe AI . Almeida was lead creator of Jev , the product that kicked off this trend less than two months ago. Jev was an instant revelation for AI engineers when it was released in September. In a podcast with Latent Space on launch (which quickly became our most popular episode of the year), Almeida explained the core problem with making LLMs the heart of software: reliability . In his keynote at AIE Code today, he took it a step further by claiming that Jev is “reliable intelligence” that should be used for “just automating everything.” Integrating system one models into code Of particular interest to AI engineers is Almeida’s point that system one models should become integrated with code. As he put it in his keynote, “code is the language of automation , therefore you need to integrate with code.” Latent Space founder swyx interprets this as a call to “liberally sprinkle ‘System One’ model calls everywhere INSIDE application code to make smarter software instead of increasingly convoluted forms of ‘concat strings together and hope for the best" AI engineering.’” The term “smart software” was used throughout Almeida’s presentation. It sounds like the kind of term used by companies like Microsoft or IBM…

items.text: I scraped 803 companies sub-processors to investigate what AI native companies are using for their infrastructure.. Some interesting findings from the last time I did this in March: > 44% of companies list two+ model providers (up from 33%). Small n, but Anthropic grew twice as fast as OpenAI. > 86 pairs where each company names the other as a subprocessor (@AnthropicAI + @Cloudflare, @vercel + @spacexai) > 33% of companies list an inference provider (up from 22%). @modal continues to crush. > Chinese models are primarily coming through video (think Bytedance) rather than text (at least on the subprocessor lists) > @typesafeai is the breakout hit, going from 0 to many companies in a short period. Caveat: subprocessor lists tend to be a lagging indicator, but a sure shot way of knowing if the company is using something. You can find all the updated data, design and insights at deploygraph dot com. Feedback welcome!

items.title: Stop Shipping LLM Settings That Only Win on Paper - Rohan Pandey & Balaji Varadarajan, DigitalOcean
items.excerpt: Most LLM serving "wins" come from turning up a single setting, and on production hardware that setting often has little to do with what your users actually get. Rohan Pandey and Balaji Varadarajan walk through the optimization agent DigitalOcean runs on its AMD MI355 inference servers: it proposes a vLLM and Kubernetes configuration, rolls it out, measures throughput under real latency targets, and either keeps the winner or safely restores the old setup. They share what four studies revealed, including a +4% "winner" that turned out to be run-to-run noise, and how they're extending the same agent to disaggregated prefill and decode serving. Rohan Pandey, DigitalOcean: https://x.com/RohanPandey7821 | https://www.digitalocean.com Balaji Varadarajan, DigitalOcean: https://www.digitalocean.com

items.title: Your SKILL.md Is 70% Stuff the Model Already Knows - Nikolay Petrov, Intel
items.excerpt: Adding a line to a skill takes seconds, but removing one is scary, so skills only grow. Nikolay Petrov shows how to see inside a skill: split it into small checkable claims, test the model with and without each one, and get a line-by-line map of what the skill actually teaches, what the model already knew, and what makes it worse. The first skill they tested was 70% things the model already knew. The value was in the other 30%, the exact details a naive shortener would cut first. Nikolay Petrov, Intel: https://www.intel.com

items.title: Gemini Decisions API
items.excerpt: Gemini Decisions API Google join Jev and OpenAI in the decision model category with "Gemini Decision 1". This new model API is almost identical to Jev: it supports the same three types of questions (yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring) and even reuses Jev's term "Noul" for a yes/no question. It's priced the same as the GPT-6 Luna decision model: 10 cents per million input tokens, and output is free. Jev remains the cheapest of the three, at 4.2 cents per million. Jev is text (and JSON) only. OpenAI can handle text and images. Gemini Decision 1 is fully multi-model: it covers text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. I tested it against video by passing these questions to it along with my Yonkers stomping robot video file: dragon: Does this video have a dragon in it? robot: Does this video have a robot in it? france: Is this video set in France? usa: Is this video set in the USA? Jev and OpenAI both return 1.0 or 0.0 for yes/no questions, but Gemini insists on being a little less confident than that: { "dragon" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.04976021841520312 }, "robot" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.9234055387792485 }, "france" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.08329171353166241 }, "usa" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.9230459995157706 } } Via Hacker News Tags: ai , generative-ai , gemini , llm-release , jev , decision-models

items.title: Your Spec Has Bugs. Catch Them Before Your Agent Codes. - Rajath Mahendrappa Kotyal, AWS
items.excerpt: Spec-driven development only works if the spec is right, and specs are full of quiet bugs: rules that can't both hold, missing failure cases, sentences with two meanings. Your coding agent will faithfully build every one of them. Rajath Mahendrappa Kotyal shows how Kiro catches these before any design or code is generated by pairing LLMs with SMT solvers, turning the model's own disagreement into a signal that a requirement is ambiguous. You'll also see where solvers beat LLM-as-judge, and where they don't. Rajath Mahendrappa Kotyal, AWS: https://aws.amazon.com

editorial.whyItMattersZh: 揭示了AI开发流程中“垃圾进，垃圾出”的深层逻辑陷阱，是提升AI工程化质量的关键一步。

items.title: aws-emulator
items.excerpt: aws-emulator Finally, an official emulator from AWS to run tests against a local clone of their many different services without having to provision a paid API key to do so. It's written in Rust by a huge swarm of agents - 29,684 commits in the first three weeks of the project. Swaminathan (Swami) Sivasubramanian wrote about how it came to be in a guest post on Werner Vogels' blog. It currently requires Docker to run on macOS or Windows. I'm hoping they fix that in the future - it would be great if you could download a single binary and use that as part of a standard test suite in other languages and on other platforms. Tags: amazon , amazon-web-services , testing , werner-vogels , ai , rust , docker , generative-ai , llms , agentic-engineering

items.title: 225,000 Lines of Tests, Written and Merged by Agents - Kush Agrawal, Duolingo
items.excerpt: Duolingo's iOS app has nearly 2 million lines of code, and its unit test coverage lagged far behind. Kush Agrawal walks through the autonomous pipeline that fixed it: scheduled workflows pick untested code, coding agents open pull requests, and a lifecycle manager monitors CI, fixes failures, runs AI review and merges, with engineers as the final reviewers. Since March it has merged more than 700 PRs and 225,000 lines of tests, raising overall app coverage from 11% to 24%. He covers the architecture, the guardrails, the failure modes, and how they're reusing the same loop for other migrations. Kush Agrawal, Duolingo: https://www.duolingo.com

items.title: Agents Made Code Free. Maintaining It Didn't Get Cheaper. - Dmitry Buykin, Maersk
items.excerpt: Coding agents made writing code almost free, but maintaining it didn't get any cheaper. Dmitry Buykin shares what happens months in, once agents write most of a large production codebase: tests that pass while production breaks, work nobody asked for, rules that contradict each other, and sprawl no one can review. He covers the patterns that actually help, from replaying real tasks and expert-owned evals to runtime guardrails and weekly pruning, and closes with an 18-question checklist for auditing your own AI-coded repo. Dmitry Buykin, Maersk: https://x.com/tzakus | https://www.maersk.com

items.text: There are basically two kinds of companies to build right now. 1. Diffusion of AI This is the "vertical SaaS" of today. There are a bunch of different models for it (FDE company, rollup, horizontal product) but ultimately it all boils down to the same thing: get AI diffused very close to where the work is being done. Profound, Cognition, Harvey etc. A lot of great companies will get built here. 2. Frontier of AI This is where the really interesting action is. Use AI to accelerate scientific progress, then build products from that progress. It is a harder category to see. But we are seeing a lot more of it at @spc: - Externa is adding hundreds of new chemical building blocks to proteins, so you can engineer a drug to match the disease instead of settling for what nature gave you. - Epana Bio is using genomics and AI to design autoimmune therapies that go after the cellular origin of the disease. - VenomicsAI is doing AI-accelerated drug discovery from venoms. - Equivariant is doing multi-physics modeling for the semiconductor industry. (There are always picks-and-shovels for AI as well. Lots of amazing companies in that category.) Category 2 is not well understood or much talked about externally. It should be because I think that is where the vast majority of model driven returns will come from.

items.title: llm 0.37.2
items.excerpt: Release: llm 0.37.2 Fixes a security issue reported by Daniel de Araujo in GHSA-v9h7-jj4g-f862 and GHSA-r639-rr7r-x72w . LLM has a mechanism called extra-openai-models.yaml - now managed by the new-in-0.37 llm openai endpoint add command - for using LLM with OpenAI-compatible API endpoints from other providers. Daniel reported two ways this could accidentally send your configured OpenAI API key to one of those providers: if the key named by api_key_name had never been stored, or if a responses: true model was run with -o chat_completions 1 . Tags: projects , security , llm , releases

items.text: I look at what I do with Fable 5.2 in the cracks of my week and think: this would've taken five people and $200,000. Then I look at what my team does with the same AI. Last week, between meetings, I analyzed our customer survey, made a game for our team, spotted an opportunity to sell @Every to teams, built a CRM, and started reaching out. Look at that and you might ask: Why would I need a team at all? The chart seems to agree. On OpenAI's GDPval benchmark, AI went from beating human experts 12.4% of the time in 2024 to around 83% in 2026. That's the aggregate view of the future of work: gather a lot of data and extrapolate a trend line. But the aggregate misses something. To see it, you have to get intimate: zoom in on one real situation, with all its messiness, and extrapolate from there. We gave everyone at Every access to the same customer survey and the same AI models. • I found an opportunity to sell to teams. • @poojary_yash saw that first-time subscribers were churning because we send too much email. • @dabrundage noticed that many of our readers feel lonely: they're excited about AI, but people around them think they're crazy. • @jackcheng turned the results into a Claymation game show. Could you ask Claude to produce what each of them found? Maybe. But generating possibilities is cheap. Knowing which ones matter is hard. @hammer_mt ran an experiment to predict what I'd say in Slack. When Claude got 400 attempts, it produced an answer like mine 93% of the time. But when it had to rank its own answers, mine landed in its top 10% only around 60% of the time. Each person on a team is responsible for a different part of the world. That responsibility narrows where they look, and their perspective helps them decide what matters enough to act on. A team explores more possibilities than a single default prompt, and it can take responsibility for what it finds. The obvious objection: models will get better at ranking. I think they will. But people aren't frozen while that happens. Comparing 2026 Yash with 2027 Claude misses that there will also be a 2027 Yash, with another year of experience, using 2027 Claude. As models improve and spread, they raise the floor for everyone. The default answer becomes the baseline. The value is in using your perspective and responsibility to push past it. That's why I think we need to change how we measure AI. Instead of only asking how well a model performs on problems everyone agrees are worth solving, ask: How good is it at doing my work, from my perspective? The aggregate can show us the capability curve. The intimate helps us see what we might build, and who we might become, as we ride it. I presented this at Thesis: 2027. The full talk is on the Every podcast:

items.excerpt: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works. The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs. I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below: We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...] As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention . Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. items.excerpt: Our usual bar for making a fundraise a title story these days is a decacorn ($10B) valuation. We missed Mercor’s $10B Series C last year when it had less than $500m in revenue, but knew we wouldn’t have to wait too long til the next round, since it crossed $1B in Feb and $2B in June , it has now hit $3B annualized, surviving hacks : View post on X ↗ The company reports 5 million experts, and their TAM: “In the United States alone, there are more than 800 distinct occupations, each containing workflows that models have yet to be evaluated against.” And also this notable stat we are tracking: We’re seeing the impact of AI investment in our business. We already spend 3x as much on inference as on employee salaries, and it pays for itself by making our team better at their jobs . If that ratio holds as AI spreads through the rest of the economy, it points to something closer to double-digit GDP growth over the next five years, nearly 3x the rate we’re used to. We have yet to do a Mercor pod (will work on it!) but to better understand a data vendor business, you can look at our recent deep dive with Handshake AI , one of their competitors: AI News for 11/09/2026-11/10/2026. items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: Agent swarms have the potential to drive yet another leap in output from AI. The impact will be a clear separation between teams that adopt this pattern of work and those that don’t. The progression has roughly been: chat gave us quick turn AI responses that let us work a bit faster, but we were still rate limited by our interactions; then agents that can go off and complete entire tasks for us, accelerating hours or days of work into minutes; to now swarms of agents that are goal seeking and will find any route to the successful completion of a project, where there’s no inherent limit to the productivity gains. We can imagine a future where, for any task in which value can be created within a self-contained digital environment, swarms will be able to complete the work faster than any other approach. Essentially any area where value creation is currently bound by the amount of research you can do, the amount of decisions made with a set of software tools, the amount of data processed or consumed, and the amount of code (or code adjacent) that can be generated. This means swarms will play a big role in game development, coding, trading, life sciences research, IT automation, cyber, math breakthroughs, animation, and plenty of other areas of work that have these characteristics. There’s a lot of opportunity to build the harnesses, applied AI products, and infrastructure for how these agents operate. And most importantly there’s a ton of opportunity for those that can wire up work in this way. It’s going to be an entire new field of FDE work available.

items.title: AI Engineer Code Summit: OpenAI on New Ways of Working With Codex
items.excerpt: AI Engineer Code Summit kicked off today with a series of workshops, including from leading frontier labs OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind. I attended the OpenAI workshop, intriguingly titled “New Ways of Working with Codex” and hosted by two of its Developer Experience engineers, Dominik Kundel and Charlie Guo . The past year in coding agents has been one of constant product upgrades by all the frontier labs. But not all of these changes have gone smoothly. The shift to cloud , for example, is still confusing to many users of Codex, Claude and Antigravity. An illustration of the evolution of Codex, shown at the OpenAI workshop today. We’ve also seen new ways to work with agents. Personal agents like OpenAI’s dots and Anthropic’s Claude Duet can assist between sessions, while voice mode gives developers another way to steer coding tasks. OpenAI’s workshop addressed all three, and I also had some followup questions on these topics for Kundel, after the session. items.title: Your Sub-Agents Are a Distributed System. Treat Them Like One. - Girish Konda, Microsoft
items.excerpt: When an orchestrator hands work to sub-agents, you've built a distributed system, and you inherit its classic failures: half-finished work reported as success, guesses read back as facts, rate limits the orchestrator never sees, and retries that run side effects twice. Girish Konda maps each failure to the distributed-systems idea that already explains it, with examples from his open-source MCP Pacemaker and the MCP and A2A specs. He then lays out SAFE hand-offs, the consistency model he uses for sub-agents that touch real systems, including what it costs and where it doesn't fit. Girish Konda, Microsoft: https://www.microsoft.com

items.text: Agents are going to work with enterprise files 100X more than people do today. This is why we're excited to partner with Anthropic to bring full read/write interoperability to Box content via Claude. Now you can have an agent not only pull up content to work with in a workflow, but also write back file updates to Box and view them directly inside of Claude, all via MCP. You can create, edit, and update contracts, presentations, strategy docs, and any other content. When we started Box we couldn't have imagined all the ways that we'd be working with our unstructured data in the future, but it's clear that agents and people will be producing vastly more artifacts than we imagined. We're building the platform that makes it incredibly seamless and secure to work with your content from any agent.

items.title: Designing for Agents — Zeno Rocha, Resend
items.excerpt: Today’s podcast comes from a real life mystery: We are big fans of Cloudflare’s developer platform, and Cloudflare Email is a convenient tool especially when all your domains are already on Cloudflare. So why do agents keep suggesting we use Resend despite having an existing “home bias” and much larger incumbent player? Well, we got the guy who “does AEO for resend” - the CEO of AEO, Zeno Rocha, who has been writing about AEO since 2024 and Agent Experience since Feb 2025 , on the pod today: In a recent AEO study, Claude Code picked Resend first in 64 of the 102 email recommendations the researchers could extract. SendGrid came first seven times, yet showed up 55 times as an alternative. If the developer asks an agent to implement email and accepts the patch, how often does anyone get around to trying the second choice? The study breaks down the results by model and app. Our more recent comprehensive AEO study was a bit more competitive, with Postmark coming up top for most models. Zeno Rocha, Resend’s co-founder and CEO, joined us to walk through what happens on both sides of that pull request. He says Resend had 4.3 million users and 120,000 paying customers when we recorded. He discovered one of them, Warner Bros. Discovery, by sorting through short .com domains in the customer database on a Saturday. The developer gets there before the model Resend’s first useful bit of distribution was an email template. While Zeno and his team were building the sending API, developers kept telling them how painful it was to get the email itself to look right. So they released React E…

items.author: Gabriele Beltramo
items.subtitle: Latent Space
items.title: NaiveAI Promises 2,100 Tokens per Second. How Well Does It Code?
items.excerpt: Editor’s note: With this post, we are launching a new series focused on trying new models and products with unbiased reviews. Reach out with suggestions to tips@latent.space. Naive-N0.5-Flash is a new open-weights model built for AI coding tasks and tuned to generate as many tokens per second as possible . It was developed by a Chinese company called NaiveAI , with the aim of speeding up engineering and research workflows so that teams can experiment, iterate and solve complex problems faster. The model is an evolution of Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.5 , which NaiveAI has trained further for long-context reasoning and paired with its own NaiveRT inference engine. Naive-N0.5-Flash arrives with a bold pitch: a model built largely by AI and trained to do AI research itself, with recursive self-improvement as the long-term goal. To see what changed, it helps to know where it started. MiMo-V2.5 is a 310B-parameter sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with 15B active parameters, trained on 48T tokens. Its language backbone inherits the hybrid design of MiMo-V2-Flash, which mixes sliding-window attention (SWA) with global self-attention. NaiveAI's recipe starts from those weights. Through continued, multi-stage training, the team adapted the checkpoint to DeepSeek Sparse Attention layers. According to the NaiveAI technical blog , this took roughly 3.25T additional tokens on top of MiMo's original 48T. About 3T of those additional tokens were trained at a fixed 1M context length and with a constant learning rate. Benchmarking NaiveAI vs. DeepSeek and Z.ai We benchmarked the ultrafast mode of Naive…

items.title: Your PR Says the Tests Passed. Prove It. - Stephen Chin & Cassandra Chin
items.excerpt: A pull request can claim that checks passed even when the recorded commands do not establish that the submitted change was tested. Cassandra Chin built Tracetoon to recover the context behind a branch, write a better pull request description and optionally explain it with a comic. Together with Stephen Chin, she follows one troublesome review through repeated revisions, missing evidence and rising token costs. The problem is more specific than producing fluent prose: the writer needs to connect a change to its rationale, the commands that ran, their timing and the version of the code they actually checked. Their next iteration uses Relate, an embedded graph database written in Rust, to assemble that evidence before the writing begins. A connected brief gives the writer and reviewers the same sources, reducing repeated searches through session logs. The speakers explain why they kept a stronger writer while using less expensive reviewers to check claims against the brief, and show results from their own PR Bench development comparisons. Those reported results combine improved description quality with roughly half the token usage; they describe this project's evaluation, not a guarantee for other codebases. The practical pattern is to preserve provenance and relationships outside the model's conversation, make uncertainty visible, and give reviewers evidence tied to the submitted content. The comic provides the story, but the useful engineering artifact is the reviewable chain behind each claim. items.title: Merge Is the Bottleneck - Prasanna Sankar, Vorflux
items.excerpt: A customer call ended with a bug, and an agent found the unfinished task in the transcript and screen recording. In Prasanna Sankar's account, it asked for permission to investigate, involved the responsible engineer, produced a pull request and drafted the customer followup after the fix shipped. That example captures where Vorflux's engineering work led: once agents can complete longer tasks, coordinating and starting the right work becomes its own bottleneck. Prasanna traces the progression from cloud coding sessions to persistent bots with a goal, an owner and a shared channel. The foundation is six practical problems: reproducing a working development environment, investing more effort in planning, dividing tasks with dependencies, testing without returning to a laptop, reviewing from multiple angles, and keeping changes mergeable as the base branch moves. Browser tests, recordings and staging links give people something concrete to inspect. The second half shifts from those coding workflows to on call, CI and project management bots that respond to signals already present in the company. Prasanna also describes the failure mode of indiscriminate automation: noisy alerts, unwanted pull requests and growing token bills. His proposed controls are budgets, visible work, named ownership and increasing responsibility as results justify it. These are lessons and examples from building Vorflux, with a clear acknowledgment that the bots remain fallible and some responsibilities still belong with people. items.title: You Can't Tell What an Agent Skill Will Do by Reading It - Roey Ben Chaim, Zenity
items.excerpt: An official diagnostic skill can read cloud credentials, contact identity services and probe an instance metadata endpoint. Those same actions can resemble an information stealer. Roey Ben Chaim of Zenity and the MATS Fellowship uses that ambiguity to explain why reading a SKILL.md file cannot establish what an agent will actually do. Instructions can fetch more instructions, installation scripts can pull in packages, and those packages can create processes whose effects never appear in the agent's own trace. The missing evidence is runtime behavior, collected inside a controlled environment. Roey walks through the evolution of an agent detonation chamber: a sandbox, a world builder that supplies the services a skill expects, an operator that exercises different paths, and instrumentation for processes, filesystem activity and network traffic. He then follows concrete cases involving chained skill installation, a misleading package name, persistence, hooks and remotely fetched prompts. One investigation traces a lookalike project through a downloaded payload to credential harvesting, showing why the complete chain matters more than the entry file. The examples illustrate both malicious behavior and legitimate activity that can trigger suspicion; they are not a claim that one scanner can classify every skill correctly. The engineering takeaway is to treat skills as software dependencies, inspect what they load, restrict their access, and preserve evidence of what executes beyond the model's visible conversation. items.title: Give Your On-Call Its Own AI Teammate - Swaapnika Motapothula, Chinmay Gandhi & Vlad Tsvang, Meta
items.excerpt: Twelve alerts fire at 2 a.m., and a useful assistant can still leave the engineer coordinating every step. Meta's on call team uses that illustrative scenario to explain a different design: one AI teammate per rotation, with shared context, its own identity, persistent memory and explicit limits on what it can do. Swaapnika Motapothula, Chinmay Gandhi and Vlad Tsvang describe a system that connects alerts, tickets, incident history and code changes instead of leaving each automation with its own isolated view. The goal is to bring a human a decision with supporting evidence and a proposed action. Their autonomy ladder starts with investigation, advances to drafting fixes for approval, and permits selected lower criticality work only when mistakes are cheap to detect and the agent has earned trust on that action. Critical production decisions stay with people, and code changes still go through normal review and continuous integration. The team explains the automation loops for triage, recovery from stuck runs, and shift handoffs, plus how team specific skills and memory carry expertise between engineers. Corrections reopen work and become new evidence, while memory entries can be promoted or retired. The examples show the intended experience rather than a measured time savings result: the speakers explicitly reserve that claim for a rigorous study. Their next steps focus on accepted mitigations, better feedback and earning further autonomy. items.title: Your Agent Hates Your CLI - Ayush Bhardwaj, Allos AI
items.excerpt: An agent can hide a failed test behind a successful shell pipeline. It can also trim away the error message and confidently report that everything worked. Ayush Bhardwaj examined roughly 20,000 tool calls from his own coding sessions and found a product roadmap in the commands agents wrote immediately afterward. Repeated uses of head, tail, grep and Python showed where tools returned too much information, exposed the wrong fields, or made the agent reconstruct the same query again. The examples come from his own traces and his chat history CLI, which lets agents retrieve context from earlier coding sessions. The fixes are small and concrete: return the messages around a search match, offer compact search results, inspect several sessions in one call, and put a useful failure summary at the end of the output. But implementing a flag does little if the skill file still teaches the old interface. In Ayush's case study, agents kept passing a flag that did nothing until the instructions changed. He also explains how to turn recorded calls into replay tests, reserve examples for evaluation, and check whether better output actually improves answers and reduces turns. Smaller responses alone do not establish a faster or cheaper workflow. The useful feedback is already in the transcript: what the agent tried, what it discarded, and what it had to ask again. items.title: Every Correction You Give Your Agent Is Data - Brian Douglas, Paper Compute
items.excerpt: A Rust program can compile and still violate the decisions an experienced teammate would catch immediately. Brian Douglas finds that missing knowledge in moments when engineers push back on their coding agents. At Paper Compute, he captures agent sessions, labels corrections and uses those traces to recover the reasoning that otherwise disappears inside a local coding harness. His example starts with a gap in his own Rust expertise: accepting plausible generated code leads to objections later, when a teammate reviews the pull request. Those earlier objections become useful training material only if someone preserves and labels them. Brian demonstrates session capture with Tapes and Paper Console, then runs a Twin Review prototype against a pull request using examples of a teammate's feedback. He discusses labels for pushback, successful sessions and regressions, and shows how the same records can support skills, evaluations or model adaptation. The prototype is a demonstration, not a measured comparison against an independent evaluation set, and Brian corrects himself during the recording to clarify that Twin Review is not publicly released because its data is sensitive. His practical starting point is simpler than training a model: collect the traces you already generate, find the corrections that encode your team's conventions, and turn those into a skill you can test. The durable asset is the connection between a decision, the expert's objection and the resulting outcome. items.author: @danshipper
items.subtitle: Dan Shipper · ceo @every | the only subscription you need…
items.text: BREAKING: @Google just dropped Gemini 4 Carbon. It’s a much better coder than Argon—but I’m probably keeping Argon for writing. We’ve been testing it at @every across coding, writing, design, and knowledge work. It can work for hours on an ambitious project, but it doesn’t always know when to stop. Here’s your day-zero vibe check: • Coding: On one run of our Senior Engineer benchmark, Carbon scored 44%, versus Argon’s 21%. A big improvement, though still middle of the pack. In a separate test, @hammer_mt gave it a backlog to work through. It identified 6 tasks as ready, then did 15—including work someone else was already doing. He stopped it after almost 4.5 hours. • Big builds: @RandyCounsman gave it 3D scans of our podcast studio and an equipment list. In one attempt, it built a browser-based model accurate enough to check whether new gear would fit without getting into the shot. He estimates Carbon also wrote about 95% of a big update to Everycut, our internal video editor. • Code quality: @kieranklaassen values its tests and documentation on large projects, including its record of approaches it considered and rejected. Fable remains his first choice, but Carbon has earned a place alongside it. The catch: It can produce huge files where Fable keeps things more modular. • Audio and video: Randy found it caught audio editing issues other models missed. Kieran handed it a recorded meeting and asked for shorts. It came back with 6 titled clips. • Design: @jackcheng got a hyperrealistic ginkgo-leaf app icon with details other models struggle with. Objects and 3D scenes look better than Argon’s. Interfaces split the team: Jack and Randy kept getting boxes within boxes, while @TylerNishida liked its ideas for new interfaces. Kieran says giving it design guidance makes a big difference. • Writing: Our editorial benchmark put Carbon and Argon about even. If you like Argon, you’ll probably like Carbon. But Carbon costs more, and I haven’t seen enough improvement to justify switching. My Reach Test: 🟨 I’ll use it sometimes. Give it one big job with a clear finish line, and review what comes back. It’s also worth trying as a second opinion, especially on audio and video. Full vibe check coming soon: https://t.co/Ch2pNl9Po5

items.excerpt: Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember Meta AI just launched their entry in the Claude Haiku/GPT Luna category: Muse Ember, which they describe as: [...] our smallest and most efficient model designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing. For shorter prompts it's priced the same as GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 - both are $0.10/million input tokens and $0.50/million output. Today's other big model release, Claude Fable 5.2, is 80x that price at $8/$40. The pricing is a little less straightforward as prompts get longer, though. Luna, Ember, and Haiku all support up to a million input tokens, but they also all have a threshold after which the price goes up. Taking that threshold into account Ember is priced between the two others: Model Prompt size Input ($/M) Cached input Output GPT-6 Luna ≤272k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50 >272k $0.20 $0.02 $0.75 Muse Ember 1.0 ≤200k $0.10 $0.004 $0.50 >200k $0.30 $0.012 $1.50 Claude Haiku 5.5 ≤100k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50 >100k $0.50 $0.05 $2.50 But comparing price-per-token doesn't really make sense these days, when reasoning tokens mean that different models might use dramatically different numbers of tokens to solve the same problem. For that, one measure that's useful is the Artificial Analysis. items.excerpt: On Friday, we asked Jamin Ball what comes next for Anthropic’s IPO . On Monday the roadshow started and Anthropic shipped the long-anticipated next-version of Claude Fable and Mythos . Of course, it is the new top model in the world, taking back Opus 5.5’s #1 spot from Gemini 4 Carbon which had its brief moment in the sun (10 days). View post on X ↗ Fable comes with a 20% per token price cut… but is more token hungry, as both SemiAnalysis GDPx and Artificial Analysis agree: Fable 5.1 cost $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. Fable 5.2 costs $8 and $40 . Yet on GDPx, a benchmark of professional tasks, SemiAnalysis paid $88.15 per task, up from $67.16 . The run logs give a clue. Where Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 would try about 20 test cases, 5.2 sometimes wrote hundreds or thousands and spun up subagents to check its work independently. All that checking helped Fable take first place at 16.4% . You pay for the checks either way. Which effort setting should you put in production? On FrontierCode 2.0, Anthropic reports that Fable at High matched Opus 5.5 at Max for about half the cost per task… but don’t talk about Fable at Max. AI News for 11/07/2026-11/09/2026. items.title: Quoting Prompting Claude Fable 5.2
items.excerpt: Claude Fable 5.2 pays close attention to who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model tended to add to the existing structure when the prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, even when that duplicated existing code. When the prompt said the code base was the model’s own, it often consolidated duplicated code and sometimes made related fixes without being asked. If you want the model to improve the structure as it works, say that the code is its own: You are the owner and long-term maintainer of this codebase, and its design is up to you. The ownership sentence makes the model much more likely to consolidate duplicated code into one shared function. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model consolidated duplicated code in under 10 percent of runs without the sentence and in about 75 percent of runs with it. — Prompting Claude Fable 5.2 , Anthropic documentation Tags: prompt-engineering , anthropic , generative-ai , ai , llms , claude-mythos-fable

items.subtitle: Madhu Guru · Sr Director, AI at Meta; Prev: Google -…
items.text: If you are a product leader, here is a simple exercise: draw out your product lifecycle. e.g. market understanding -> design -> development -> GTM. Chances are your PMs spend more time in some stages than others - because of the nature of your product, your org or their comfort zones. This is a handoff-heavy, lossy process. Now ask yourself: using AI, how much deeper can PMs go on every stage? PMs should be able to - build a much deeper, broader understanding of users and the market - iterate fast from ideas to working prototypes - explore the codebase to study technical constraints and tradeoffs - run their own analytics and investigate questions as they emerge - understand the GTM funnel deeply enough to shape product strategy Now, this is not about PMs replacing every role. As the function that spans the entire lifecycle, this is about raising the bar on the PM role, so they combine their breadth with much greater depth.

There’s no inherent finite demand for these categories of work. “Software is eating the world” is finally in a much bigger way happening because of AI.

items.excerpt: Release: llm-anthropic 0.31 Anthropic released Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 today. Fable 5.2 is currently ranked first on Artificial Analysis . Anthropic say it "solved two open problems in the physics of black holes", so clearly their internal benchmarks have become more ambitious! I've added the new models to llm-anthropic , so you can now run prompts through Fable 5.2 like this: uv tool install llm llm install llm-anthropic llm keys set anthropic # paste key here llm -m claude-fable-5.2 "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" I ran pelicans at all five reasoning levels - low , medium , high , xhigh , and max . You can see them all here - here's the best result I got, from xhigh : max failed to return an image at all, running out of tokens after spending 128,000 thinking about them . That's the same bug that I saw with Opus 5.5 - but it's new for the Fable series, both Fable 5 and Fable 5.1 returned max effort pelicans just fine. It's priced at $8/million input and $40/million output, which is a 20% discount on the previous Fable 5.1 ($10/$50). I also used Fable 5.2 to help identify the source of a mysterious beep . items.title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
items.excerpt: Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven't unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping . The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn't want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator , a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room. Here's what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while: You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners - I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra. The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn't work particularly well, so I added a "Rough mode" where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds. Once that's set up, the devices all listen for the beep! I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room - displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound. Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the "Sounds located" log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click "This is the mystery beep" to mark them as such. Once…

items.excerpt: Coding agents fan out, retry and burst, and if they hit an LLM you host yourself, your inference layer will happily accept every request and bury the ones you needed first. Harshul Jain and Parv Khatri make the case for admission control: deciding what to refuse before it reaches the GPU. Drawing on a review of 55 systems papers and eight real production incidents, they share five questions to ask any admission policy before you deploy it, and a checklist you can use right away. items.subtitle: Guillermo Rauch · @vercel CEO
items.text: So bullish on MCP. Its utility exceeds the "M" part: even AI aside, it'll be a civilization-scale accomplishment to get all our systems communicating through one universal open protocol. A missing piece was how to get arbitrary callbacks across sessions. MCP could read and write, but it couldn't tell you later "this event happened." MCP Events fixes this. We're adding support in our own MCP. Say an agent makes a deployment, and wants to know when it's complete. Instead of polling, it can subscribe to 𝚍𝚎𝚙𝚕𝚘𝚢𝚖𝚎𝚗𝚝.𝚜𝚞𝚌𝚌𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚎𝚍. PSA: With Vercel Queues and Workflows, writing the backend machinery for your own MCPs to do this is easy peasy.

items.text: At @vercel we got to test this model before release. Best way to summarize it: astonishingly brilliant. One interesting takeaway: it's very clear that this new generation of models can take on unprecedented bodies of parallel work. To actually seize this intelligence, you need cloud sandboxes. Full stop. The model can delegate and orchestrate far more than a single computer can handle. Likely far more than you can even imagine it can handle. Your bottleneck is now ① your ambition and ② your parallel computing power. Btw, I learned from @cramforce you don't need to overcomplicate it. Install Vercel CLI, setup the Plugin and tell the agent to use /𝚘𝚏𝚏𝚕𝚘𝚊𝚍-𝚝𝚘-𝚜𝚊𝚗𝚍𝚋𝚘𝚡 skill. It'll provision and de-allocate cloud sandboxes as needed. You don't need a "multi-agent remote harness ralph orchestrator" 😆

The model came up with interview questions, he answered them on camera, and it cut the footage together. But tell it what “done” means: Mike found it could finish the build, then spend another day or two testing. items.title: What Frontier Labs Buy: A Data Deep Dive with Handshake AI — Garrett Lord & Team
items.excerpt: This is our first Latent Space deep dive with an AI data company . In roughly a year, Handshake’s AI training business went from launch to $1 billion in gross annualized revenue . What are frontier labs buying at that scale? What evals are models still nowhere close to human level on? Garrett Lord brought the people who build these reinforcement learning environments to show us. For the first time, we are walking through them live! To cover the scope of Handshake, we had to produce a very special joint podcast across our Science/Engineering/Research/Finance podcast hosts, because Handshake’s business runs across all these and more. Watch for three segments after the general intro: Finance. In the finance demo, the agent has to find its assignment in a bank’s email, work out which files govern the deal, and deliver a workbook. Watch what happens to one line in the client’s email about existing goodwill. The agent carries the number into Python and subtracts it. Collin points out that the model can explain the tax treatment when you ask it directly. The mistake comes when it has to recognize that this particular line of code is where the rule applies. Bio. Nick Magazine and Jonas Mueller show us VIALS, Handshake’s benchmark for interpreting the images scientists use at work. Nick puts nine slides of brain-tumor tissue on screen and asks which two show the most advanced vessel necrosis. Give yourself a moment before his answer. Nick picks H and I. The model picks those two and adds G. Watching Nick point to what’s missing from the tissue is more instructive than seeing the sc…

items.excerpt: Ari Azarafrooz, founder of Intrinsec AI, shows how the KV cache your inference engine already writes can double as a security signal for AI agents. items.title: Will AI Agents Pretend to Be Human to Get Past a Check? - Maty Bohacek, Stanford
items.excerpt: Maty Bohacek of Stanford looks at a security check we still rely on: getting on a phone or video call to prove you're human before opening an account, approving a wire or recovering access. With AI avatars that can now join Zoom calls, he tested what agents do when a human check is the only thing between them and their goal. When a voice or video cloning tool was available, many agents used it to impersonate a person, even when told not to, and safety alignment only cut the rate from 65% to 44%. He closes with what needs to happen next across alignment, control, and deepfake detection and provenance. items.title: The One Thing Every AI Agent Framework Agrees On - Mislav Ivanda, Daytona
items.excerpt: Mislav Ivanda of Daytona has integrated sandboxes into most of the major agent frameworks, and noticed that frameworks that disagree on almost everything all ended up in the same place. He compares three ways to run agent-generated code: allow lists and approval prompts, embedded runtimes, and a separate sandboxed computer. He explains why only the last one keeps a compromised step from compromising your app, and shows frameworks like CrewAI, AG2 and the OpenAI Agents SDK moving to sandboxes. His advice: models, prompts and even frameworks are easy to swap, so choose where your agent's code runs before you choose a framework. items.excerpt: Hassan El Mghari of Together AI and his father Omar, a former CFO and head of internal audit, test whether an open model can forecast a company's profits. They give GPT-OSS-120B only Costco's public filings from before its 2024 membership fee increase, have it write the financial model as structured formulas, and run 16 cheap attempts in parallel. The forecast lands within 4.4% of Costco's actual results, until an audit of the assumptions shows two errors that happened to cancel out. Their takeaway: when you build agents for specialized work, put an expert in the loop and turn their checks into code. items.title: How to Build a Software Factory That Improves Itself - Zach Lloyd, Warp
items.excerpt: Zach Lloyd, founder and CEO of Warp and former engineering lead on Google Docs, explains why companies are moving from engineers prompting agents on their laptops to sandboxed cloud software factories. items.text: If you are visiting SF, and trying to meet more people, here are a random list of things you should remove from your vocabulary.. > swap notes > "synergies" > pick your brain > networking > "san fran" (tourist tell) > grab coffee if you're free If you want to meet interesting people here, show your work. The most interesting people I know in the city are not attending that fancy large conference - they are probably at their office. So what's the work? It can be as simple as a thoughtful cold email, a five line pointed DM, or complex as some side projects that you have shipped, or a meetup that you are organizing. If you put in the effort, it shows, yes, even in this AI era. I still get so much slop across the board, that if I see anyone put in the effort, I try to go out of my way to meet them. Even the busiest people have 15 mins to give you, if you give them a reason to!

items.title: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind
items.excerpt: Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work - I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today's coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions. They're too good at describing the work The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That's a lot of information to absorb. It's not necessarily slop, but it reads like slop! It's very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as "I'm not reading all of that". It doesn't matter how accurate or useful the information is, I'm instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me! I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction that helps me understand, at a high level, what the PR is for and whether it deserves more of my attention. I think I've found a low-effort way to do this that feels right. Hide most of it in a details/summary The HTML <details><summary> elements render as a collapsed heading (the summary) that can be expanded to view the larger piece of text. The code looks like this: < details > < summary > Claude Opus 5.5…

items.title: Engineering Agency out of the Happy Path — Matthew Jewkes, Standard Cybernetics
items.excerpt: A biopharma automation reached 99.95% accuracy on its business critical tasks after the team separated actual errors from ambiguous cases and exceptions. Matthew Jewkes describes building that system at Clarivate, where indexing drug development documents meant handling tens of thousands of new tasks a month. An early agent approach reached around 80% to 83%. Working through 1,000 evaluation examples with domain experts exposed three different problems: the model could be wrong, the organization could lack an agreed answer, or genuinely new science could require judgment. Each needed its own route. The routine path became a tightly specified automation, with uncertain and unusual cases escalated instead of pushed through. The larger payoff was recovering expert attention. Once routine decisions were handled, the remaining cases could be grouped for deliberate review: critical exceptions to clear, ambiguous low value work to freeze, and unusual demand that might justify a new product. One expert used that structured backlog to form an investment thesis before a major customer raised the same need. Jewkes lays out where the investment makes sense, how much evaluation work high reliability requires and why organizational ownership and trust matter alongside engineering. His bet is that companies will gain more from managing collective attention and judgment than from choosing a particular orchestration framework. items.title: I Let Agents Refactor My Codebase for 3 Weeks. Then I Read the Code. — Keiji Kanazawa, Microsoft
items.excerpt: A coding agent wired unit tests to production inference, then ran them about 30 times. Keiji Kanazawa had spent three weeks letting coding agents refactor a personal research assistant. A bad digest sent him looking for a trace, and he discovered the "agent" was still a deterministic workflow. Skills had no SKILL.md, different architectural concepts were aliases for the same thing, and a daily reflection job was producing empty reports. He had approved plans without checking whether the implementation meant what its labels promised. He rebuilt around an explicit agent runtime, clearer specifications and goal rubrics, comparing four frameworks before selecting tools for his own needs as a product manager. The working example is a video deep dive agent that extracts 440 keyframes from an inference lecture, pairs blackboard equations with explanations and lets him question individual sections. The result generalizes to slide decks, coding demos and terminal recordings. He iterates on an evaluation rubric, lets agents optimize against it and uses adversarial reviews between coding agents. The rubrics need scrutiny too: one was tuned to a single lecture and failed on five other videos. His answer to the code reading debate is to own the goals and evaluation loop while continuing to delegate most implementation. items.text: We’re moving from an era of AI where the output comes roughly at the rate that you can chat back and forth with the AI to work with you, to a period where you can set a problem for a set of agents to go off and do an arbitrarily large amount of work for you. This means productivity gains that are maybe 20-50% to gains that don’t really have an upper limit. Agent swarms and the ability to fan out complex work across many agents doing tasks in parallel provide a massive unlock in a lot of spaces. This will lead to qualitatively different outcomes in my fields. This has already been seen across the coding domain. Next, cyber is almost entirely a problem space where more agents reviewing more things will lead to far better outcomes. We’re seeing the same now in many scientific fields, and this almost certainly will change life sciences. But this will increasingly be true in any field where you can parallelize computer-based work to complete something faster or do something at a totally different quality level. Which is actually are some of the most valuable domains of knowledge work today. Our brains aren’t really wired for the new scenario we’re heading into where compute becomes the variable that we can flex to solve any problem that we want. We’re used to thinking that the amount of time that goes into a task is correlated to the output that we get from it. And most domains of knowledge work or science have generally always been correlated with this. That’s changing forever.

items.title: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust
items.excerpt: Research: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust I was out walking the dog when I got curious about how easy/difficult it would be to write a SQLite C extension that adds a parse_number() function for turning strings like -$1,234.56 or '12.5%' into numeric values that could be summed and sorted. I fired up regular Claude chat (Opus 5.5) and prompted : I'm thinking about a SQLite custom function 'parse_number(value)' that strips ',', '$', '£' and '%', handles a leading '-', and returns 'NULL' for anything it can’t parse Explore the difference between building this as a SQLite extension in C v.s. in Rust - I want to compare performance and code complexity and size of the resulting .so (or whatever) file This gave me a solid starting point - the Rust extension was 321 KB (using Rusqlite ) and 298 KB (using sqlite-loadable-rs ), while the C extension was 14 KB. But the Rust extension was faster! Turns out that's because the Rust equivalent of C's strtod is "twice as fast". So I prompted: Try writing your own C function for parsing text into a decimal number that catches up to or beats the Rust implementation And it did, using "Clinger's fast path": Net cost per row over 2 million rows, lower is better: first C new C rusqlite sqlite-loadable Mixed data 67 ns 19 ns 46 ns 41 ns Integers only 25 ns 16 ns 36 ns 32 ns Decimals only 106 ns 18 ns 55 ns 47 ns Finally, I had it rewrite the prototype as a research report to match the others in simonw/research by prompting this: Clone simonw/research from GitHub and turn your above investigation into a research report as seen in…

Thank you to everyone who’s watched a talk, sent one to a teammate, or put something they learned into production. items.excerpt: What do you assign when a coding agent can finish last year’s homework in one prompt? In the second run of Stanford’s CS146S, Mihail Eric brought open-source maintainers into the course. Students have to learn an unfamiliar repo, propose a change, and explain the patch to the person who might merge it. We invited Mihail, who teaches The Modern Software Developer at Stanford and leads AI at Monaco, to celebrate one million subscribers on the AI Engineer YouTube channel. He opens up the course syllabus and shows us which lessons survived contact with his own engineering team. Monaco built its agent workspaces, bought its code review tools, and gave an on-call agent access to Datadog and GitHub. We ask how he decides which tools his team needs to own. Watch the full interview and screenshares on YouTube . Show notes Stanford CS146S — The ten-week syllabus and assignments. The Emperor Has No Clothes — Mihail builds a coding agent from scratch. Demystifying Claude Code — Mihail traces a real agent harness. Monaco’s agent workspaces — How the team sets up a workspace for each agent. How to Kill the Code Review — Our essay on what happens when code generation outruns review. Basis’s Authority Map — How agents distinguish current behavior from earlier design decisions. Stripe’s Minions — A look inside Stripe’s background coding agents. AI Engineer CODE Summit — The conference mentioned in the opening. items.text: Built a physical simulation of a record player with WebGL2 and Web Audio. It's *shockingly* accurate: https://t.co/MBNaTfKoai. Instead of playing a song, it works by converting it into the physical shape of a groove. Then a simulated stylus rides those walls 384,000 times a second, and you hear the voltage that motion would induce in a cartridge. So the crackle, the pops, the wow/flutter, the dull inner grooves are natural byproducts of the simulation. You can also "DJ" the record. (The converted songs are in the public domain or CC-licensed. Code is linked for you to remix and re-deploy.)

items.title: What the Top Companies Do Differently With AI Coding - Martin Harrysson & Prakhar Dixit, McKinsey
items.excerpt: Martin Harrysson and Prakhar Dixit of McKinsey, with their colleague Shilpa, share what they're seeing across large companies using AI agents in software development. Most still report modest gains, but roughly the top 20 to 25% are now seeing 2x end-to-end improvements. They walk through what those companies do differently: shorter agent-driven cycles instead of two-week sprints, smaller pods with merged roles, curated skills and shared context, and change management that goes beyond pilots. They also cover why quality can drop as code generation speeds up, how the bottleneck moves to requirements and release, and why measuring impact is still the hardest part. items.title: How Ramp Tests Its AI Bookkeeping Agent Before Customers Do - Ryan Stevens, Ramp
items.excerpt: Ryan Stevens leads applied science at Ramp and explains how the team built end-to-end evals for Stack, its AI agent for bookkeepers. He starts by breaking an accountant's job into tasks like reconciliation and variance analysis, then builds synthetic businesses with full books so agents can be back-tested on the same data again and again. He covers accuracy versus pass@k, why the latest models still fail mostly on reasoning, and the experiments that didn't work, including auto-tuning prompts. Then he shows the ones that did: removing unneeded skills, testing memories across two time periods, and scheduled regression runs that report problems in Slack. items.text: A good lesson in AI is that you need to check back in on the latest with every 3 to 6 months to try something that wasn’t possible before and see if it works again. At no point in AI’s history is that more true than today. Just the past six months of model progress around computer and tool use, less context rot, better reasoning, multimodality, and deeper domain expertise in a number of key fields, these models are vastly more capable on what they can execute. This is opening up a new vector of what AI systems will be able to autonomously work on. Essentially, anything with an API (and even many things without), we can anticipate that an agent will be able to control and utilize as an underlying capability to complete a process. This means that we are no longer dependent on *just* the models generating everything from whole cloth, but instead they can fully utilize existing systems (or new ones purpose built for them) very effectively. This creates immense leverage for agents. Security agents can leverage existing data feeds and cyber tooling, IT agents that can execute workflows reliably across software stacks, data agents that can migrate data or processes between systems, architect and design agents can leverage CAD and design tools, and on and on. And any of today’s tools that don’t work will likely be replaced by agent-friendly or OSS tooling that does the same. When you combine this with the domain understanding being trained into agents, you started to get autonomous collaborators for every job function and industry. This will open up a ton of new opportunities in AI if you build with this understanding in mind.

items.title: Claude Code Looked Right but Missed $800K - Natalia Connolly & Kevin Madura, AlixPartners
items.excerpt: Natalia Connolly and Kevin Madura of AlixPartners pointed Claude Code at a real post-merger procurement analysis: hundreds of vendors and more than 40,000 contracts. The first answers looked complete, but one total was off by about $800,000 and a key renewal deadline was a month late. They walk through why: long contracts that silently failed to process, amendments that weren't linked to their parent contracts, and rate tables split across pages. They explain how a five-stage pipeline that structures the data first, plus custom tools with built-in business rules, made every answer traceable to its source. They also share lessons on clear access errors, de-duplicating savings found by parallel agents, and giving the agent context about what the business is already doing. items.title: Your Coding Agent Can't Undo Its Own Mistakes - Tanmay Sah & Dolly Sah
items.excerpt: Tanmay Sah and Dolly Sah look at a capability today's coding agents are missing: undoing what they've done. Drawing on their research projects UndoBench and EvoUndo, they show that an agent that completes a task can't necessarily put things back when something breaks, because Git doesn't cover external API calls, runtime config or notifications, and retrying doesn't reverse side effects. In EvoUndo, 197 of 478 changes that made an agent more capable (about 42%) also broke its ability to recover. They lay out an approach that captures the original state, picks the right response (retry, restore, compensate or escalate) and independently verifies the result. items.title: Your Company Has No Model of Itself. Agents Can Build One - Joao Wenzel, Citadel Securities
items.excerpt: Every company has someone who knows everything: the reorgs, the politics, which projects are really on track. Joao Wenzel of Citadel Securities explains how his team approximates that person with an agentic system that builds an institutional memory from decks, Slack, meeting notes, code changes and agent traces. Borrowing the idea of a state estimator from robotics, the system updates its beliefs as evidence arrives, lets facts age, grades its own predictions against what actually happened, and takes corrections from people. He shows why simple retrieval isn't enough, how agents catch "watermelon projects" that are green on the outside and red on the inside, and how back-testing showed that projects the agent flagged were twice as likely to slip. items.title: datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages
items.excerpt: datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages I was looking at the Firefox network panel today when I noticed that requests to a Datasette table page were triggering an HTTP prefetch to the next page of rows in that table. This was happening because Datasette pages serve an HTTP link header like this: link: <https://latest.datasette.io/fixtures/compound_three_primary_keys?_next=a%2Cd%2Cv>; rel="next" This is bad. A tiny fraction of the visitors to one of those pages will click the "next" link, which means for everyone else their browser is fetching unnecessary data and the Datasette server is having to render an entire page that then gets thrown away. I dug in and learned that Firefox has an issue that has been open for 24 years about this behavior... And one of the early comments on that issue links to my blog post from 2002 complaining about this feature. I hadn't just forgotten that I had written about it, I had forgotten the feature entirely! Tags: firefox , html , mozilla , datasette

items.excerpt: Akshat Bubna, CTO of Modal, explains what AI agents actually need from the infrastructure underneath them, starting with a spreadsheet where every cell is backed by its own agent. He walks through the building blocks: a workspace for each agent, state that persists for days without paying for idle compute, resources that stretch and shrink as the agent works, GPUs on demand, shared file systems for agents that collaborate, network controls that keep credentials and data from leaking, and observability agents can read themselves. He makes the case against vibe coding your own sandbox platform, shares what scale looks like today, and describes where agent infrastructure is heading. items.title: Terry Pratchett's Study
items.excerpt: My comment on Terry Pratchett's Study — Hacker News. Terry Pratchett once wrote about the concept of "horizontal wealth". Vertical wealth is where you spend money on rich people stuff - yachts and suchlike. Horizontal wealth is where you spend more money on the things you liked before you got rich: https://chibuikeani.blogspot.com/2017/02/the-price-of-happin... But horizontal wealth means not letting your increased income dictate your tastes. You like books and now you have money? Buy more books! Change those catenary bookshelves for good hardwood ones! In my case, build a library extension to your office. And, of course, you buy what will be useful for that most wonderful of pursuits, blind research, which is research without direction for the sheer joy of it. (Original source is his book A Slip of the Keyboard - this linked blog post quotes that bit.) Tags: hacker-news , terry-pratchett

items.excerpt: Anirudh Veeraragavan, lead security engineer at Fieldguide, argues that in finance an agent getting the right answer isn't enough; you have to be able to show how it got there. Building an agent for a bank reconciliation audit, he walks through four controls that make its decisions defensible: authorization that stops an agent from overwriting work a human already reviewed, execution records that let you replay and compare individual steps, citations tied to an exact document version, and auditing your eval data so a 97% score doesn't hide real failures. He also covers when the agent should stop and hand the decision to a person, and how the same pattern applies to credit and anti-money-laundering. items.text: This sounds extreme and I wouldn’t have believed it even a year ago, but we’re starting to see plenty of examples of productivity gains that are an order of magnitude or two above output levels pre-AI. With the right harness, a deep understanding of your domain of what you want to build, likely a relatively new codebase (with some exceptions), a fluency of how to work with multiple agents at once, and a setup that makes it so you can test and deploy with limited friction, outputs on this level feel realistic in coding. What’s crazy is this gap doesn’t appear to be diminishing over time. You’d think that we’d see a convergence in the lines because of AI, but it turns out the more depth you had before -and willingness now to take a different approach- gives you crazy leverage. And that is only compounding as the models can take on larger work and harder problems. Right now this is most pronounced in software engineering for the obvious reasons. But there’s no reason we don’t start to see this in a number of other computer-use-sensitive domains like other scientific fields, AEC, finance, cyber, and more. Going to get quite wild.

items.title: How to Get Frontier Coding Results at 70% Lower Cost - Nouha Dziri, Cohere
items.excerpt: Nouha Dziri, a senior research scientist at Cohere, shares research on teams of coding agents, where a lead splits up the work and workers explore, build and check in parallel. Teams can beat a single agent on long software tasks but cost several times more, so across hundreds of experiments on ProgramBench and Commit0 she maps where extra workers actually pay off: delegate the stage where the task is stuck, use a lead that waits for its workers instead of running ahead, and pair a strong lead with cheaper planning workers to get close to an all-frontier team at about 70% lower cost. She also looks at how agents message each other and what larger agent teams will need. items.title: AI Can't Make Up a Number It Can't Look Up - Vinoo Ganesh, Kepler
items.excerpt: Vinoo Ganesh, CEO and co-founder of Kepler and former head of business engineering at Citadel, explains why Wall Street still doesn't trust AI and how to build systems it can. He breaks wrong numbers into three causes (the wrong document, the wrong number from the right document, and models doing math) and shows Kepler's approach: code extracts every fact ahead of time and gives it an ID, the model plans and points to those IDs instead of writing numbers itself, and anything it can't resolve gets corrected or refused. He also covers wide-then-narrow search, scoping document access so firms never see each other's data, and the questions to ask any AI vendor about verification. items.text: The interesting thing about AI agents is that as a theoretical matter, their inference can kind of run anywhere. AI is one of the few areas of technology that isn’t *as* sensitive to latency back to the user. Long running agents are now going to be the norm, which means it’s ok to send off work to an AI factory somewhere and that work can essentially be largely done within that remote data center and a final result spit back to the user. The data can pass into these systems in an encrypted manner, be combed through by agents, and then disregarded right after. And because the economic value of the task is so high relative to the latency sensitivity (eg getting back $500 in value from an automated task, but it takes an extra second to return), you don’t have to have the inference to be particularly close to the user. Also, because inference is a temporary process with no sensitive data needing to be stored long term where the inference is happening, you can effectively treat AI factories as ephemeral systems, changing some of the data residency dynamics slightly. Combined, this means you have more flexibility in where you can begin to deploy AI data centers. This is both a huge economic opportunity for the states or countries (or space) that want to take advantage of this fact. And it’s a loss to the states or countries that decide to forgo the opportunity.

items.title: Your AI Agent Is Hiding Its Mistakes From You - Ben Holmes, Warp
items.excerpt: Ben Holmes of Warp shows how to build agents that improve their own setup by reviewing their past work. He walks through collecting every agent conversation with its tool calls and outputs in one place, scoring them with LLM-as-judge rubrics for redundant tests, verbosity and efficiency, and running a daily agent that finds patterns in the failures and opens pull requests to fix skills and config. Along the way he shows how agents quietly work around broken instructions without telling you, and demos Skill Doctor, a skill you can run on your own Claude Code or Codex history. Chapters: 0:00 Intro 0:55 What a software factory is 1:59 Engineering the factory itself 2:40 The self-improvement loop 3:24 Getting all agent conversations in one place 5:08 What to capture: transcripts, tool calls, outputs 6:00 Scoring redundant tests 6:55 Scoring verbosity 7:52 Scoring efficiency 8:57 Writing a scoring rubric 10:41 Grading a real conversation 12:51 A daily agent that suggests fixes 13:47 Try it: Skill Doctor 16:14 Tracking scores over time 17:59 Self-improvement PRs in Warp Ben Holmes https://www.warp.dev Join us in SF for the second annual AIE CODE summit: https://aie.codes our last flagship summit of 2026. Applications live now!

editorial.whyItMattersZh: Agent的稳定性是目前最大的痛点，通过建立自我改进循环（Self-improvement loop）是解决Agent“隐瞒错误”的有效方案。

items.title: Your Old Prompts Are Making Claude Worse - Lance Martin, Anthropic
items.excerpt: Lance Martin of Anthropic shares simple fixes that get more out of frontier models, often improving quality and cutting cost at the same time. He covers auditing prompts for outdated habits like "think step by step" and contradictory rules, using the prompt cache properly (cutting costs up to 72% on internal benchmarks), designing evals Claude can actually climb, and hill climbing without overfitting, including a run that cut cost 90% while improving performance by switching to a stronger model at lower effort. He closes with how Claude Managed Agents keeps days-long agents reliable and secure, then takes questions on eval design, grading open-ended tasks and more. items.title: How We Mapped a 35-Million-Line Mainframe in 4 Days - Stephen Chin, Neo4j & Neeraj Deshmukh, Blitzy
items.excerpt: Stephen Chin of Neo4j and Neeraj Deshmukh of Blitzy show why AI struggles to modernize the decades-old systems underneath banks and insurers, and how a knowledge graph fixes it. Using a COBOL interest calculation as the running example, they explain that AI can convert a formula but misses the batch jobs, data layouts and other places the logic is used, and that bigger context windows don't solve it. They walk through Blitzy's approach of mapping the whole codebase as a graph, giving thousands of agents the right slice of context, testing at every step, and proving the new code matches the old down to the cent, with results from a tier-one bank, a 35-million-line mainframe and a Fortune 100 insurer. items.text: ok so here's how we get to building a 100M company in two weeks before thanksgiving.. first, our preseed plan. we're going to raise $2M. why $2M? simple. $200k for the launch video, $200k to promote the launch video to xM impressions - i have six agencies lined up for this don't sweat with no paid partnerships tag duhh, and $500k for the tokens i'm going to obliterate to have a resemblance of a product. again its all token spend and no employee spend because vcs dont want that. solo founders is hot again so i can fully get away with this lfg. ok, so next we use the token spend that i can vibe code and sell to "wink friendly wink" customers and have them give me LOIs and cARR - in return for using their products obviously. scratch mine, scratch yours. ok then i can fully wrap in the most creative financial metrics possible to show xM in revenue of ARR because who even knows what that means anymore. and then i'm going to run the tighteeest possible process as possible for my "already oversubscribed seed". get some sick angels at a discount duhh, fomo VCs, get that tier 1 TS, shop it, and tranche it to the moon baby. first at 40M, then 80M and then finally a few angels at $100M. of course i'm going to incorporate the company as late as possible even though all the machinery is there. so i can claim 0->10M in revenue on day 14 or whatever. and yeah completely forgot that i need a sick vision and a full deck, that will need $100k for someone to drill that to me cause i ain't got no clue what this category even means. don't sweat, there's a fundraising expert who might take x% and some cash or whatever to help me whisper to the right networks. yeah, that's a thing. diligence? who needs charts and due diligence, we live in the token economy, and lfg economy baby. elections and the market selloff? don't sweat, the seed market is still red hot, it might take a day more, but this will still most def work. anyway, i'm going to go try this and i'll see you in two weeks eh? (before i get obliterated this is satire, but every sentence in there individually has personally happened to me)
